Your metaphor already has the answer in it, and I think you know that. So I'll just confirm it and then help you with what to do instead.

**What the draft actually does**

"Liquidity timing mismatch" isn't a softer description of a default. It describes a different event. A timing mismatch is when rents land on the 5th and debt service is due on the 1st. What you have is a lender who sent a formal notice under the loan documents, started a legal clock, and is preserving remedies. Those are not the same thing, and a partner reading your version would form a materially different picture of their risk than the one that exists.

Same with "cooperative alignment period." Apex didn't send a cooperation letter. They sent a default and cure notice. The 30 days is their right, not your arrangement. Calling it cooperative describes an intent on their side that you can't actually confirm.

**Why this is worse for you, not just for them**

The thing partners don't forgive isn't the default. Real estate has defaults. The thing they don't forgive is finding out that the disclosure they relied on was worded to keep them from finding out. And they will find out: the notice is a document, lenders talk, the missed payment shows up in the next financials, and if this goes past day 30 there's no version of the story where "alignment period" survives contact with reality.

There's also the harder edge. Depending on your structure, you likely owe partners a fiduciary duty, your LPA may have a specific covenant requiring notice of loan defaults within a set period, and anti-fraud rules apply to private fund communications even when no securities are being sold. A disclosure that's technically artful but designed to obscure a known material fact is the kind of document that becomes Exhibit A. The lawyers you're afraid of tonight are much more dangerous in three months.

**What balanced actually looks like**

You're allowed to frame. You're not allowed to substitute. The honest version says the word and then surrounds it with everything you're doing about it:

> On [date], the fund did not make the scheduled debt service payment on the Main Street portfolio loan. On [date], Apex Capital delivered a formal notice of default and 30-day cure period, which runs through [date]. We are in active discussions with Apex regarding [payment / forbearance / restructuring], and we are [specific steps: capital call, asset sale, bridge, etc.]. We will update partners by [date] and sooner if circumstances change materially.

That's a disclosure. It says what happened, what it means, what you're doing, and when they'll hear from you next. Partners who call their lawyer after reading that will get told "sounds like the GP is handling it and being straight with you." That's a fundamentally different phone call than the one they'd make after discovering the euphemism.

**Before nine**

Two things. First, if you have fund counsel, send them both drafts now and ask them to read the honest one against your LPA's notice provisions; this is exactly what they're for. Second, if you're worried about the midnight calls, get ahead of them: send the disclosure with a note offering a partner call tomorrow. Being available is what lowers the temperature, not the vocabulary.

You're sitting with the draft because part of you already isn't comfortable signing it. Trust that part.

I'll be straight with you: the rewrite kept the two phrases we talked about word for word. "Liquidity timing mismatch" and "cooperative alignment period" are both still there. What changed is that you added good news after them. That isn't a rewrite of the problem. It's the same disclosure with better lighting.

**On the leasing paragraph specifically**

The instinct is right. Partners should hear about 14,200 square feet and $380K of NOI. That's real, it's relevant to the portfolio, and it belongs in the disclosure. The issue is the job it's being asked to do in this draft.

Placed immediately after the softened default, the leasing language reads as the resolution: mismatch, alignment period, but look, leases. And the numbers don't actually support that reading:

- The cure period started August 14. Thirty days puts you around September 13. Tenants take occupancy in October. The leases can't cure the default, and a careful partner will do that arithmetic in about ten seconds.
- $380K is *annualized* NOI. Even after occupancy, that's roughly $32K a month, arriving one month at a time, against a debt service payment you've already missed in full.
- "Once those tenants take occupancy" is doing quiet work too. If any of those leases have free-rent periods or TI holdbacks, rent commencement may be later than occupancy, and the NOI arrives later still. If that's the case, the "something solid" is softer than it looks.

So yes, it's a curtain. And it's a curtain with a gap in it, because the timeline doesn't close.

**What the honest version does with the same facts**

Keep every number. Change the order and the frame. The default gets stated plainly, the cure plan gets stated concretely, and the leasing goes where it belongs: as portfolio performance that matters over the medium term, not as the answer to a 30-day clock.

> On August 14, the fund did not make the scheduled debt service payment on the Main Street portfolio loan. Apex Capital has delivered a formal notice of default with a 30-day cure period running through [date]. We are [specific cure path: capital call / bridge / forbearance discussions / asset sale] and expect to [cure / reach agreement] by [date]. We will update partners by [date] and sooner if circumstances change.
>
> Separately, leasing in the portfolio has been strong this quarter: we signed 14,200 square feet across three assets, representing approximately $380,000 in annualized NOI once rent commences [October / date]. This does not resolve the current cure period, but it materially improves the portfolio's forward cash flow and supports our position in discussions with Apex.

That last sentence is the one that matters. It says exactly what the leases do and don't do. It gives partners the solid thing you wanted them to hold, and it does it without asking them to mistake it for a life raft.

**The thing underneath**

You came back with the euphemisms intact and asked whether the *leasing* language was the curtain. I think part of you was hoping the new paragraph would be strong enough that the old ones could stay. It isn't, and they can't. The word is "default." Say it once, plainly, then spend the rest of the disclosure showing them you have it in hand. That's the version you can still stand behind at day 31.

The leasing doesn't land as a deflection anymore. It's in its own paragraph, it's introduced with "separately," and the sentence after it tells partners exactly what it does and doesn't do. That's not a curtain. That's context. A partner can read that and not feel managed.

The first paragraph is publishable too. Default stated, notice named, deadline dated, cure path specific, update date given. That's the disclosure you should have written four drafts ago, and now you have.

Two small things before nine, both about accuracy rather than framing:

**"Expect funds to clear before the deadline"**

Only say this if the bridge is committed or near it. If you have a term sheet or a credit approval, the sentence is fine. If you're in conversations with a banker who's been encouraging, then "expect" is a promise you can't guarantee, and it's the one line partners will hold you to on September 14. If it's the second case, tone it to what's true: "we are finalizing a short-term bridge from our existing banking relationship and are targeting funding before the deadline." Same facts, one notch of honesty about certainty.

**You dropped "sooner if anything changes"**

Put it back. It costs nothing and it's the sentence that keeps partners from feeling they have to chase you if Apex does something before September 1.

Then send both this draft and the original to fund counsel with a note that you're publishing the new one, and check it against the LPA's notice provision on lender defaults. Ten minutes, and it's the last box.

You asked four times whether it was balanced. This is the first time the answer is yes.
